reminder: The ideal class group is the group of fractional ideals modulo the principal fractional ideals.
definition: Let $R$ be a [Dedekind domain](c:dedekind-domain). Its ideal class group $\mathrm{Cl}(R)$ is the [quotient group](c:quotient-group) of the group of nonzero [fractional ideals](c:fractional-ideal) of $R$ by the subgroup of [principal](c:principal-ideal) fractional ideals. Its order, when finite, is the class number, and it is finite for the [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) of a [number field](c:number-field).
examples: For every [principal ideal domain](c:principal-ideal-domain), such as $\mathbb Z$, the class group is trivial.
The ring $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ has class group of order $2$, because the ideal $(2,1+\sqrt{-5})$ is not principal.
The ring of integers of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-23})$ has class number $3$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$ is not a Dedekind domain, so its nonzero fractional ideals are not all invertible and do not form a group, and this construction does not apply.

steps: In a Dedekind domain $R$, every nonzero fractional ideal is an invertible module of rank one.
Two fractional ideals are isomorphic as modules exactly when they differ by a principal fractional ideal.
So the quotient by the principal fractional ideals is the group of isomorphism classes of invertible modules.
That group is the [Picard group](c:picard-group) $\mathrm{Pic}(R)$, so $\mathrm{Cl}(R)=\mathrm{Pic}(R)$.
links.why: The class group of a Dedekind domain is a Picard group, so Picard group tools apply to it.

steps: Take a number field $K$ and the trivial modulus $\mathfrak m=1$, with no real places.

The [ray class group](c:ray-class-group) modulo $\mathfrak m$ is the group of fractional ideals prime to $\mathfrak m$, modulo the principal ideals $(\alpha)$ with $\alpha\equiv1\bmod^\times\mathfrak m$.
For $\mathfrak m=1$, every ideal is prime to $\mathfrak m$ and every $\alpha$ satisfies the congruence.
So the ray class group of modulus $1$ is the ideal class group of $K$.
links.why: The class group is the coarsest ray class group, so ray class fields refine the Hilbert class field.

reminder: An idempotent morphism is an endomorphism $e$ that squares to itself, so $e\circ e=e$.
definition: In a [category](c:category), an idempotent is an [endomorphism](c:endomorphism) $e\colon X\to X$ of an [object](c:object) $X$ whose [composition](c:composition) with itself is $e$, that is $e\circ e=e$. In a category with one object, this is an idempotent element of the endomorphism [monoid](c:monoid).
examples: Every [identity morphism](c:identity-morphism) $\mathrm{id}_X$ satisfies $\mathrm{id}_X\circ\mathrm{id}_X=\mathrm{id}_X$.
In the category of vector spaces, the projection $(x,y)\mapsto(x,0)$ of $\mathbb R^2$ onto the $x$-axis is idempotent.
In the category of sets, the map $n\mapsto\max(n,0)$ on $\mathbb Z$ is idempotent.
Non-example: the rotation $R$ of the plane by $90^\circ$ has $R\circ R=-\mathrm{id}$, which is not $R$, so $R$ is not idempotent.

steps: Take a [projector](c:projector) $P\colon V\to V$ on a vector space $V$, so $P\circ P=P$.
A linear map is a morphism of the category of vector spaces, so $P$ is an endomorphism of the object $V$.
It composes with itself to give itself, so $P$ is an idempotent of that category.
links.why: A fact proved for idempotents of any category applies to projectors, such as a splitting into image and kernel.

reminder: Two functions are identically distributed when they push their measures forward to the same measure.
definition:
Let $f\colon\alpha	o\gamma$ be a [measurable function](c:measurable-function) on a [measure space](c:measure-space) $(\alpha,\mu)$, and let $g\colon eta	o\gamma$ be measurable on $( eta,
u)$, with the same target $\gamma$. They are identically distributed when the [pushforward measures](c:pushforward-measure) agree, $f_*\mu=g_*
u$, that is $\mu(f^{-1}(B))=
u(g^{-1}(B))$ for every measurable $B\subseteq\gamma$. The two domains may be different spaces; for [random variables](c:random-variable) this says that they have the same law.
examples: A standard normal variable $X$ and $-X$ are identically distributed, although they differ at every point where $X\ne0$.
The first toss of a fair coin on one probability space and the last toss of a fair coin on another space are identically distributed.
The outcome of a fair die roll and the outcome $7-X$ of the same roll have the same law.
Non-example: a fair coin toss $X$ and the constant variable $0$ have different laws, so they are not identically distributed.

steps: Take random variables $X_1,X_2,\dots$ that are [independent and identically distributed](c:iid-random-variables).
Forget the independence condition and keep only the equality of their laws.
Any two of them then push the probability measure forward to the same measure, so they are identically distributed.
links.why: A statement about identically distributed variables holds in particular for an iid sequence.

reminder: An induced subgraph keeps some vertices of a graph and all edges of the graph between them.
definition: Let $G$ be a [graph](c:graph). A [subgraph](c:is-subgraph) $H$ of $G$ is induced when every [edge](c:edge) of $G$ whose two ends are [vertices](c:vertex) of $H$ is also an edge of $H$. So $H$ is fixed by its vertex set $S$, and one writes $H=G[S]$.
examples: Delete one vertex of a $4$-cycle: the three remaining vertices with their two edges form an induced path.
Every induced subgraph of a complete graph is complete.
The graph $G$ is an induced subgraph of itself, with $S$ the whole vertex set.
Non-example: delete one edge of a triangle but keep all three vertices. The result is a subgraph, but it is not induced, because the deleted edge joins two kept vertices.

steps: Take an induced subgraph $H$ of $G$.
Its vertices and edges are vertices and edges of $G$, so $H$ is a [subgraph](c:is-subgraph) of $G$.
The induced case adds one condition: every edge of $G$ between two vertices of $H$ lies in $H$.
links.why: Facts about subgraphs apply to induced subgraphs, which are the subgraphs fixed by a vertex set.

reminder: An infinite product $\prod a_k$ is the limit of the partial products $a_0a_1\cdots a_n$ as $n$ grows.
definition: For a [sequence](c:sequence) $(a_k)_{k\ge0}$ of [real](c:real-number) or [complex numbers](c:complex-number), let $P_n=a_0a_1\cdots a_n$ be its partial products. The infinite product $\prod_{k=0}^\infty a_k$ [converges](c:convergence) when $P_n$ has a limit that is not $0$, and its value is that limit. Some authors also allow finitely many zero factors.
examples: $\prod_{k\ge1}(1+1/k^2)=\sinh(\pi)/\pi$.
Non-example: $\prod_{k\ge1}(1+1/k)$ has partial products $n+1\to\infty$, so it does not converge.
Non-example: $\prod_{k\ge1}\tfrac12$ has partial products $2^{-n}\to0$, so it diverges to $0$.

steps: Take an [Euler product](c:euler-product) $\prod_p(1-p^{-s})^{-1}$ over the primes $p$.
List the primes in order as $p_0<p_1<p_2<\cdots$.
Put $a_k=(1-p_k^{-s})^{-1}$, so the partial products are products over the first primes.
Then the Euler product is the infinite product $\prod_ka_k$.
links.why: Convergence tests for infinite products apply to Euler products.

reminder: Intersection cohomology of a singular space counts cycles that meet the singular strata in a controlled way, so Poincaré duality holds.
definition: Let $X$ be a [stratified space](c:stratified-space), for example a complex algebraic variety, and fix a perversity $\bar p$, which bounds how much a chain may meet each stratum. The intersection homology $IH^{\bar p}_*(X)$ is the [homology](c:homology) of the complex of chains whose intersections with each stratum have a dimension bounded in terms of $\bar p$. Intersection cohomology is the dual theory, equal to the [sheaf cohomology](c:sheaf-cohomology) of the intersection complex; it equals [singular cohomology](c:singular-cohomology) for a manifold and satisfies Poincaré duality on a compact oriented pseudomanifold.
examples: For a smooth manifold with its trivial stratification, intersection cohomology is ordinary cohomology.
For a projective variety $X$, even a singular one, intersection cohomology satisfies Poincaré duality and the hard Lefschetz theorem.

Non-example: the ordinary cohomology of the suspension of a torus, a space with two singular points, has Betti numbers $1,0,2,1$, so Poincaré duality fails; ordinary cohomology is not intersection cohomology here.

steps: Take a smooth manifold $M$ with the trivial stratification, which has one stratum, $M$ itself.
No chain meets a singular stratum, so every singular chain is allowable for every perversity.
Hence the intersection chain complex of $M$ is the ordinary singular chain complex.
So the intersection cohomology of $M$ is the [singular cohomology](c:singular-cohomology) of $M$.
links.why: On manifolds the two theories agree, and on singular spaces intersection cohomology keeps duality.

reminder: The intersection number of two cycles of complementary dimension counts the points where they meet, each with an orientation sign.
definition: Let $M$ be a [closed oriented manifold](c:closed-oriented-manifold) of dimension $n$, and let $A,B$ be closed oriented [submanifolds](c:submanifold) of dimensions $a$ and $b$ with $a+b=n$, which meet [transversally](c:transversality). The intersection number $A\cdot B$ is the sum, over the finitely many points of $A\cap B$, of $+1$ or $-1$, according to whether the orientations of $A$ and $B$ together give the orientation of $M$. It depends only on the [homology](c:homology) classes of $A$ and $B$, so it extends to all complementary classes as the cup product of their Poincaré duals evaluated on the [fundamental class](c:fundamental-class) of $M$.
examples: Two distinct lines in the complex projective plane meet in one point, transversally, so their intersection number is $1$.
On the torus $S^1\times S^1$, the circles $S^1\times\{p\}$ and $\{q\}\times S^1$ meet once, so $A\cdot B=\pm1$, with the sign set by the orientations.
On the moduli space $\overline{M}_{1,1}$, the intersection number of the class $\psi_1$ is $1/24$, a rational number because the space is an orbifold.
Non-example: two circles in $\mathbb R^3$ have dimensions $1+1\ne3$, so no intersection number is defined for them.

reminder: An inverse function $g$ of $f$ undoes $f$, so $g(f(x))=x$ and $f(g(y))=y$.
definition: Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a [function](c:function). An inverse function of $f$ is a function $g\colon Y\to X$ with $g(f(x))=x$ for all $x\in X$ and $f(g(y))=y$ for all $y\in Y$. It exists exactly when $f$ is a [bijection](c:bijection), and then it is unique and written $f^{-1}$.
examples: The natural logarithm is the inverse function of $\exp\colon\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$.
On $[0,\infty)$, the square root is the inverse function of $x\mapsto x^2$.
The inverse function of $x\mapsto2x+3$ on $\mathbb R$ is $y\mapsto(y-3)/2$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto x^2$ on $\mathbb R$ has no inverse function, because it is not injective: $f(1)=f(-1)$.

steps: Take a function $f\colon X\to Y$ with an inverse function $g$.
In the category of sets, $g\circ f=\mathrm{id}_X$ and $f\circ g=\mathrm{id}_Y$.
These are the equations of an inverse of an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism), so $f$ is an isomorphism of sets.
links.why: Inverse functions are the inverses of isomorphisms in the category of sets.

steps: Regard the sets $X$ and $Y$ as discrete categories, so that the function $f$ is a functor.
A function $g$ with $g\circ f=\mathrm{id}$ and $f\circ g=\mathrm{id}$ is then a functor with the same equations.
So $g$ is an [inverse functor](c:inverse-functor) of $f$, and $f$ is an isomorphism of discrete categories.
links.why: The inverse of a function is the case of an inverse functor between discrete categories.

reminder: A well-order is a total order in which every nonempty subset has a least element.
definition: A well-order on a [set](c:set) $S$ is a [relation](c:relation) $\prec$ on $S$ that is [transitive](c:is-trans), such that any two distinct elements are comparable, and such that every nonempty subset of $S$ has a $\prec$-least element. Equivalently, it is a [total order](c:total-order) that is also a [well-founded relation](c:well-founded-relation).
examples: The natural numbers with their usual order.
Every [ordinal](c:ordinal), such as $\omega+1$, with the order $<$.
Every finite total order.
Non-example: the integers $\mathbb Z$ with the usual order, because the subset of negative integers has no least element.

steps: Take a well-order $\prec$ on $S$ and a nonempty subset $A$.
The least element of $A$ is minimal, because no element of $A$ lies below it.
So every nonempty subset has a minimal element, and $\prec$ is a [well-founded relation](c:well-founded-relation).
The well-order adds that any two elements are comparable.
links.why: Well-founded induction works on every well-order, where the minimal element is the least element.

steps: Take a well-order $\prec$ on $S$ and two distinct elements $x,y$.
The subset $\{x,y\}$ has a least element, say $x$, so $x\prec y$.
So any two elements are comparable, and $\prec$ is a [total order](c:total-order).
The well-order adds that every nonempty subset has a least element.
links.why: Every fact about total orders holds for a well-order.

steps: Take an [ordinal](c:ordinal) $\alpha$ and order its elements by membership.
Every element of $\alpha$ is an ordinal, and membership is transitive and total on ordinals.
Every nonempty set of ordinals has a least element.
So $\alpha$ with membership is a well-order.
links.why: Each ordinal is a well-order, and conversely each well-order is isomorphic to one ordinal.

reminder: An isotopy is a continuous path of embeddings, that is, a homotopy in which every stage is an embedding.
definition: An isotopy between embeddings $f,g\colon X\to Y$ is a [homotopy](c:homotopy) $H\colon X\times[0,1]\to Y$ from $f$ to $g$ such that every stage $H_t=H(-,t)$ is an [embedding](c:embedding). Equivalently, it is a path from $f$ to $g$ in the space of embeddings, which sits inside the space of [continuous functions](c:continuous-function) from $X$ to $Y$.
examples: The maps $H_t(x)=(1-t/2)x$ shrink the unit circle in the plane to the circle of radius $1/2$, and each $H_t$ is an embedding.
Rotating a knot in $\mathbb R^3$ about an axis is an isotopy from the knot to its rotated copy.
Non-example: the unknot and the trefoil are homotopic embeddings $S^1\to\mathbb R^3$, but they are not isotopic.
Non-example: passing one strand of a knot through another changes a crossing, but at that moment the map is not injective, so the path is not an isotopy.

steps: Take an isotopy $H\colon X\times[0,1]\to Y$ between embeddings $f$ and $g$.
The map $H$ is continuous with $H_0=f$ and $H_1=g$, so it is a [homotopy](c:homotopy) from $f$ to $g$.
The isotopy adds that every stage $H_t$ is an embedding.
links.why: Every isotopy is a homotopy, so homotopy invariants cannot tell isotopic embeddings apart.

reminder: The Itô integral of an adapted process against Brownian motion is the $L^2$ limit of left-endpoint sums.
definition: Let $B$ be a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) for a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal F_t)$, and let $H$ be an adapted [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) with $\mathbb E\int_0^TH_t^2\,dt<\infty$. For a simple $H$ with value $H_{t_i}$ on $(t_i,t_{i+1}]$, the Itô integral $\int_0^TH\,dB$ is the sum $\sum_iH_{t_i}(B_{t_{i+1}}-B_{t_i})$, and the Itô isometry $\mathbb E\big(\int_0^TH\,dB\big)^2=\mathbb E\int_0^TH_t^2\,dt$ extends it to all such $H$ as an $L^2$ limit. As a process in $T$, the integral is a continuous [martingale](c:martingale).
examples: $\int_0^TB_t\,dB_t=\tfrac12(B_T^2-T)$; the term $-T/2$ is the difference from the ordinary chain rule.
For a deterministic $f\in L^2[0,T]$, the integral $\int_0^Tf\,dB$ is a centered Gaussian variable with variance $\int_0^Tf(t)^2\,dt$.
Non-example: the right-endpoint sums $\sum_iB_{t_{i+1}}(B_{t_{i+1}}-B_{t_i})$ converge to $\tfrac12(B_T^2+T)$, which is not the Itô integral $\int_0^TB\,dB$.

steps: A [stochastic integral](c:stochastic-integral) integrates a process against a stochastic integrator, such as a semimartingale.
Brownian motion $B$ is a continuous martingale, so it is a semimartingale.
The Itô integral integrates adapted processes against this integrator $B$, so it is the stochastic integral for the integrator $B$.
links.why: General stochastic calculus, such as the Itô formula, applies to Itô integrals.

reminder: The Killing form of a Lie algebra is the bilinear form $\kappa(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}(\mathrm{ad}_x\mathrm{ad}_y)$.
definition: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) over a field. The Killing form is the symmetric [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) $\kappa(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}(\mathrm{ad}_x\circ\mathrm{ad}_y)$, where $\mathrm{ad}_x=[x,-]$ is the [adjoint representation](c:adjoint-representation) and the trace is that of a [linear map](c:linear-map) $\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak g$. It is invariant: $\kappa([x,y],z)=\kappa(x,[y,z])$.
examples: On $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ over $\mathbb C$, the Killing form is $\kappa(x,y)=2n\operatorname{tr}(xy)$.
On an abelian Lie algebra every $\mathrm{ad}_x$ is $0$, so $\kappa=0$.
On the compact Lie algebra $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, the Killing form is negative definite.

Non-example: the trace form $(x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(xy)$ of the defining representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ is symmetric and invariant, but it is not the Killing form, which is $2n$ times larger.

reminder: The Koszul complex of $x_1,\dots,x_d$ is the exterior algebra of $R^d$ with the differential that sends each basis vector $e_i$ to $x_i$.
definition: Let $R$ be a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) and $x_1,\dots,x_d\in R$. The Koszul complex $K_\bullet(x)$ has terms $K_n=\wedge^nR^d$, the $n$-th power of the [exterior algebra](c:exterior-algebra) of the [free module](c:free-module) $R^d$, and differential $\partial(e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_n})=\sum_{j=1}^n(-1)^{j+1}x_{i_j}\,e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat{e_{i_j}}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_n}$. It is a [chain complex](c:chain-complex), and it equals the tensor product of the complexes $R\xrightarrow{x_i}R$.
examples: For $d=1$, the Koszul complex is $0\to R\xrightarrow{x}R\to0$.
For $d=2$, it is $0\to R\xrightarrow{(-x_2,\,x_1)^T}R^2\xrightarrow{(x_1,\,x_2)}R\to0$.
When $x$ is a [regular sequence](c:regular-sequence), the Koszul complex is a [free resolution](c:free-resolution) of $R/(x_1,\dots,x_d)$.
Non-example: the complex $0\to R\xrightarrow{x_1}R\to0$ is the Koszul complex of $(x_1)$ only; it is not the Koszul complex of $(x_1,x_2)$, which has three terms of ranks $1,2,1$.

steps: The terms $\wedge^nR^d$ of the Koszul complex are [free modules](c:free-module) of finite rank.
The differential $\partial$ is $R$-linear and lowers the degree $n$ by one.
A direct check gives $\partial\circ\partial=0$ because $R$ is commutative.
So the Koszul complex is a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) of free modules.
links.why: Homology and the long exact sequence apply to the Koszul complex.

reminder: A Lagrangian is a function of positions and velocities whose time integral, the action, is stationary along real motions.
definition: In classical mechanics, a Lagrangian is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $L(q,\dot q,t)$ of coordinates $q$, velocities $\dot q$ and time $t$; for a mechanical system $L=T-V$, kinetic energy minus potential energy. A motion $q(t)$ is physical exactly when its [action functional](c:action-functional) $S[q]=\int L(q,\dot q,t)\,dt$ is stationary, that is, when it solves the [Euler-Lagrange equations](c:euler-lagrange-equation) $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}$. In constrained optimization, the Lagrangian of $f$ under the constraint $g=0$ is $f-\lambda g$.
examples: For a particle of mass $m$ in a potential $V$, $L=\tfrac12m\dot x^2-V(x)$ gives Newton's law $m\ddot x=-V'(x)$.
For a harmonic oscillator, $L=\tfrac12m\dot x^2-\tfrac12kx^2$.
To maximize $f(x)$ under $g(x)=0$, use $L(x,\lambda)=f(x)-\lambda g(x)$; the envelope theorem differentiates the optimal value through it.
Non-example: the total energy $T+V$ is the Hamiltonian, not the Lagrangian; the Lagrangian is $T-V$.

reminder: The Levi-Civita connection is the unique connection on the tangent bundle that preserves the metric and has no torsion.
definition:
Let $(M,g)$ be a [Riemannian](c:riemannian-manifold) or [pseudo-Riemannian manifold](c:pseudo-riemannian-manifold). Its Levi-Civita connection is the unique [connection](c:connection-on-a-bundle) $
abla$ on the [tangent bundle](c:tangent-bundle) that is compatible with $g$, meaning $X\,g(Y,Z)=g(
abla_XY,Z)+g(Y,
abla_XZ)$, and torsion-free, meaning $
abla_XY-
abla_YX=[X,Y]$. The Koszul formula gives it, and its [Christoffel symbols](c:christoffel-symbols) in local coordinates are computed from the metric.
examples: On $\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, $\nabla_XY$ is the ordinary derivative of the components of $Y$, so all Christoffel symbols vanish.
For a surface $S\subset\mathbb R^3$, $\nabla_XY$ is the tangential part of the ordinary derivative $D_XY$.
The [geodesics](c:geodesic) of the Levi-Civita connection are the curves $\gamma$ with $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$, such as the great circles of a sphere.

Non-example: on a non-abelian Lie group with a left-invariant metric, the connection with $\nabla_XY=0$ for left-invariant fields $X,Y$ is compatible with the metric, but it has torsion $-[X,Y]\ne0$, so it is not the Levi-Civita connection.

steps: Take the Levi-Civita connection $\nabla$ of $(M,g)$.
It is a [connection](c:connection-on-a-bundle) on the tangent bundle, so it is an [affine connection](c:affine-connection) on $M$.
The Levi-Civita case adds compatibility with $g$ and zero torsion, and these two conditions make $\nabla$ unique.
links.why: Curvature, parallel transport and geodesics defined for affine connections apply to the Levi-Civita connection.

reminder: The limit superior of sets $A_n$ is the set of points that lie in infinitely many of the $A_n$.
definition: For a sequence of [subsets](c:subset) $A_1,A_2,\dots$ of a [set](c:set) $X$, the limit superior is $\limsup A_n=\bigcap_{n\ge1}\bigcup_{k\ge n}A_k$, built from [intersection](c:intersection) and [union](c:union). A point $x$ lies in it exactly when $x\in A_k$ for infinitely many $k$.
examples: If $A_n=A$ for even $n$ and $A_n=B$ for odd $n$, then $\limsup A_n=A\cup B$.
For $A_n=[0,1/n]$, the limit superior is $\{0\}$.
For $A_n=\{n\}$ in $\mathbb N$, the limit superior is empty, because each point lies in only one $A_n$.
Non-example: for $A_n=[0,1/n]$, the union $\bigcup_nA_n=[0,1]$ is not the limit superior, because $1/2$ lies in only $A_1$ and $A_2$.

reminder: A smooth map is a local diffeomorphism when each point has a neighborhood that the map sends diffeomorphically onto an open set.
definition: A [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $f\colon X\to Y$ between [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) is a local diffeomorphism when every $x\in X$ has an open neighborhood $U$ such that $f(U)$ is open in $Y$ and $f|_U\colon U\to f(U)$ is a [diffeomorphism](c:diffeomorph). Equivalently, by the inverse function theorem, the [differential](c:differential) $df_x\colon T_xX\to T_{f(x)}Y$ is an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) at every point $x$.
examples: The covering map $\mathbb R\to S^1$, $t\mapsto e^{it}$, is a local diffeomorphism that is not injective.
The inclusion of an open subset $U\subseteq X$ is a local diffeomorphism.
The exponential map $\exp\colon\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ is a local diffeomorphism, because its derivative $e^z$ is never $0$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto x^3$ on $\mathbb R$ is a smooth homeomorphism, but not a local diffeomorphism at $0$, because its derivative is $0$ there and its inverse is not smooth.

steps: Take a [diffeomorphism](c:diffeomorph) $f\colon X\to Y$.
For every point $x$, take the neighborhood $U=X$.
Then $f(U)=Y$ is open, and $f|_U=f$ is a diffeomorphism onto it.
So $f$ is a local diffeomorphism.
links.why: Every result for local diffeomorphisms covers diffeomorphisms, which are the bijective case.

steps: Take a local diffeomorphism $f$ and a point $x$.
The differential $df_x$ is an isomorphism, so it is injective.
A smooth map whose differential is injective everywhere is an [immersion](c:immersion).
A local diffeomorphism adds that $df_x$ is also onto, so $\dim X=\dim Y$.
links.why: Facts about immersions apply to local diffeomorphisms, which are the immersions of equal dimension.

steps: Take a local diffeomorphism $f$ and a point $x$.
The differential $df_x$ is an isomorphism, so it is surjective.
A smooth map whose differential is surjective everywhere is a [submersion](c:submersion).
A local diffeomorphism adds that $df_x$ is also injective, so the fibers are discrete.
links.why: Facts about submersions apply to local diffeomorphisms, which are the submersions with discrete fibers.

reminder: A space is locally connected when every point has a neighborhood basis of connected open sets.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is locally connected when, for every point $x$, every [neighborhood](c:neighborhood) of $x$ contains a [connected](c:connected-space) [open set](c:open-set) that contains $x$. Equivalently, the connected open sets form a base of the topology.
examples: $\mathbb R^n$ is locally connected, because open balls are connected.
Every discrete space is locally connected, because each point is a connected open set.
The set $[0,1]\cup[2,3]$ is locally connected but not connected.
Non-example: the closed topologist's sine curve is connected but not locally connected, because small balls around points of its limit segment meet it in infinitely many separate arcs.

steps: Take a [locally path connected space](c:locally-path-connected-space) $X$ and a point $x$.
Every neighborhood of $x$ contains a path connected open set around $x$.
A path connected set is [connected](c:connected-space).
So every neighborhood contains a connected open set around $x$, and $X$ is locally connected.
links.why: A result for locally connected spaces covers every locally path connected space, such as a manifold.

reminder: The logarithmic derivative of $f$ is $f'/f$, the derivative of $\log f$.
definition: For a differentiable [function](c:function) $f$ with $f\ne0$, the logarithmic derivative is the quotient $f'/f$ of its [derivative](c:derivative) by $f$, which equals $(\log f)'$ wherever the [logarithm](c:logarithm) of $f$ is defined. It turns products into sums, $(fg)'/(fg)=f'/f+g'/g$. For a [meromorphic function](c:meromorphic-function), it has a simple pole at each zero and pole of $f$, with residue equal to the order of the zero, or minus the order of the pole.
examples: For $f(x)=x^n$, the logarithmic derivative is $n/x$.
For $f=e^g$, the logarithmic derivative is $g'$.
For a polynomial $P(z)=c\prod_i(z-a_i)$, $P'/P=\sum_i1/(z-a_i)$; the proof of the Gauss-Lucas theorem uses this sum.
Non-example: the derivative $f'$ is not the logarithmic derivative; for $f=x^2$, $f'=2x$ but $f'/f=2/x$.

reminder: A lower triangular matrix has only zeros above its main diagonal.
definition: A lower triangular matrix is a [square matrix](c:square-matrix) $A=(a_{ij})$ with $a_{ij}=0$ whenever $i<j$. Only the diagonal entries and the entries below the diagonal can be nonzero.
examples: Every [diagonal matrix](c:diagonal-matrix), and the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$.
The factor $L$ in an LU decomposition $A=LU$ is lower triangular, with ones on its diagonal.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ is not lower triangular, because the entry $a_{12}=2$ above the diagonal is not zero.

steps: A [triangular matrix](c:triangular-matrix) is a square matrix with zeros on one side of its main diagonal.
Choose the side above the main diagonal.
A matrix with zeros there is lower triangular, so it is a triangular matrix.
links.why: Facts about triangular matrices apply to the lower case, which fixes the side of the zeros.

steps: Take a [diagonal matrix](c:diagonal-matrix) $D=(d_{ij})$, so $d_{ij}=0$ whenever $i\ne j$.
Then $d_{ij}=0$ in particular whenever $i<j$.
So $D$ is lower triangular.
Lower triangular matrices also allow nonzero entries below the diagonal.
links.why: Every diagonal matrix is lower triangular, so results for lower triangular matrices cover diagonal ones.

reminder: A manifold with boundary is a space that looks near each point like an open piece of the closed half-space.
definition: A manifold with boundary of dimension $n$ is a [Hausdorff](c:hausdorff-space), [second-countable](c:second-countable-space) [topological space](c:topological-space) in which every point has an open neighborhood [homeomorphic](c:homeomorphism) to an open subset of the half-space $\mathbb H^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:x_n\ge0\}$. The boundary $\partial M$ is the set of points that such a homeomorphism sends to $x_n=0$; this set does not depend on the choice.
examples: The closed ball $D^n$ is a manifold with boundary the sphere $S^{n-1}$.
The interval $[0,1]$ has boundary $\{0,1\}$, and the closed Möbius band has boundary one circle.
The half-space $\mathbb H^n$ is itself a manifold with boundary $\{x_n=0\}$.

Non-example: a closed disc with a segment attached at one boundary point is not a manifold with boundary, because the point where the segment joins has no neighborhood like an open piece of a half-plane.

steps: Take a [manifold](c:manifold) $M$ of dimension $n$.
Each point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open ball of $\mathbb R^n$.
An open ball is homeomorphic to an open ball inside $\{x_n>0\}$, which is an open subset of $\mathbb H^n$.
So $M$ is a manifold with boundary, and its boundary is empty.
links.why: Statements about manifolds with boundary hold for manifolds, which are the case with empty boundary.

reminder: A maximal torus of a compact Lie group is a torus that lies in no larger torus.
definition: Let $G$ be a [compact](c:compact-group) connected [Lie group](c:lie-group). A [torus](c:torus) in $G$ is a connected compact [abelian](c:abelian-group) [subgroup](c:subgroup), isomorphic to $U(1)^k$. A maximal torus is a torus that no other torus of $G$ properly contains; all maximal tori are conjugate, and their common dimension is the rank of $G$.
examples: In $U(n)$, the diagonal matrices $\mathrm{diag}(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ with $|z_i|=1$ form a maximal torus of dimension $n$.
In $SU(2)$, the matrices $\mathrm{diag}(z,\bar z)$ with $|z|=1$ form a maximal torus, a circle.
In $SO(3)$, the rotations about a fixed axis form a maximal torus, a circle.
Non-example: in $U(2)$ the circle $\{\mathrm{diag}(z,1)\}$ is a torus, but it is not maximal, because it lies in the diagonal torus $U(1)^2$.

steps: Take a maximal torus $T$ of $G$.
By definition $T$ is a connected compact abelian subgroup, so $T$ is a [torus](c:torus) in $G$.
The maximal case adds that no torus of $G$ contains $T$ properly.
links.why: A maximal torus carries everything known about tori, and it is unique up to conjugacy.

reminder: A measure-preserving system is a probability space with a map $T$ such that $\mu(T^{-1}A)=\mu(A)$ for all measurable $A$.
definition: A measure-preserving system $(X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)$ is a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\mu$ on a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) $(X,\mathcal B)$ together with a [measurable map](c:measurable-function) $T\colon X\to X$ such that $\mu(T^{-1}A)=\mu(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal B$. In other words, the [pushforward measure](c:pushforward-measure) $T_*\mu$ equals $\mu$, so $\mu$ is an [invariant measure](c:invariant-measure) of $T$.
examples: The rotation $x\mapsto x+\alpha$ of $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with Lebesgue measure.
The doubling map $x\mapsto2x\bmod1$ on $[0,1)$ with Lebesgue measure.
The shift on $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}$ with a product measure.
Non-example: the map $x\mapsto x^2$ on $[0,1]$ with Lebesgue measure does not preserve the measure, because $\mu(T^{-1}[0,a])=\sqrt a\ne a$.

steps: A [measure-preserving map](c:measure-preserving-map) is a measurable map $f\colon(X,\mu)\to(Y,\nu)$ with $f_*\mu=\nu$.
Take $Y=X$, $\nu=\mu$ and $f=T$.
The condition $T_*\mu=\mu$ says that $T$ is a measure-preserving map from $(X,\mu)$ to itself.
So a system is a probability space with one measure-preserving self-map.
links.why: Facts about measure-preserving maps apply to the map $T$ of a system, and $T$ can be iterated.

steps: Take an [ergodic map](c:ergodic) $T$ of a probability space $(X,\mu)$.
An ergodic map is measure-preserving, so $\mu(T^{-1}A)=\mu(A)$ for every measurable $A$.
So $(X,\mu,T)$ is a measure-preserving system.
Ergodicity adds that every invariant set has measure $0$ or $1$.
links.why: Results for measure-preserving systems cover ergodic ones, which are the indecomposable systems.

reminder: A mixed strategy of a player is a probability distribution over the pure strategies of that player.
definition: In a game where player $i$ has a [finite set](c:finite-set) $S_i$ of pure strategies, a mixed strategy of player $i$ is a [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) $\sigma_i$ on $S_i$, that is, numbers $\sigma_i(s)\ge0$ for $s\in S_i$ with $\sum_s\sigma_i(s)=1$. The payoff of a profile of mixed strategies is the [expected value](c:expected-value) of the payoff when the players choose independently.
examples: In matching pennies, playing heads and tails with probability $1/2$ each is a mixed strategy, and it is the equilibrium strategy.
In rock-paper-scissors, the mixed strategy $(1/3,1/3,1/3)$ is the equilibrium strategy.
Every pure strategy is a mixed strategy that puts probability $1$ on one choice.
Non-example: weights $(0.5,0.7)$ on two pure strategies sum to $1.2$, so they are not a mixed strategy.

reminder: A modular tensor category is a braided fusion category with a ribbon structure and an invertible S-matrix.
definition: A modular tensor category is a [fusion category](c:fusion-category) $\mathcal C$ over $\mathbb C$ with a braiding and a [ribbon](c:ribbon-category) structure whose S-matrix is invertible. The S-matrix has entries $S_{ij}=\operatorname{tr}(c_{Y_j,Y_i}c_{Y_i,Y_j})$, the trace of the double braiding of two simple objects $Y_i,Y_j$. Equivalently, the braiding is nondegenerate: only direct sums of the unit object braid trivially with every object.
examples: The Fibonacci category, with simple objects $1$ and $\tau$ and $\tau\otimes\tau=1\oplus\tau$.
The category of graded vector spaces over a finite abelian group $A$, with the braiding from a nondegenerate quadratic form $q\colon A\to U(1)$.
The modular quotient of the representations of the [quantum group](c:quantum-group) $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ at a root of unity.

Non-example: the representation category of a nontrivial finite group, with its symmetric braiding, is braided fusion but not modular, because every object braids trivially and the S-matrix is degenerate.

steps: Take a modular tensor category $\mathcal C$.
Its definition includes a braiding $c_{X,Y}\colon X\otimes Y\to Y\otimes X$ on a monoidal category.
So $\mathcal C$ is a [braided monoidal category](c:braided-monoidal-category).
The modular case adds fusion, a ribbon structure and an invertible S-matrix.
links.why: Braided monoidal category tools, such as the hexagon equations, apply to modular tensor categories.

steps: Take a modular tensor category $\mathcal C$.
By definition, $\mathcal C$ is a [fusion category](c:fusion-category): it is semisimple, rigid and has finitely many simple objects.
The modular case adds a braiding, a ribbon structure and an invertible S-matrix.
links.why: Fusion rules and dimensions are defined for every modular tensor category.

reminder: Monadic second-order logic extends first-order logic with quantifiers over subsets of the universe.
definition: Monadic second-order logic over a relational signature has the formulas of [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic), with variables for elements. It adds set variables $X,Y,\dots$, atomic formulas $x\in X$, and quantifiers $\exists X$ and $\forall X$ that range over all subsets of the universe. It has no quantifiers over relations of arity $2$ or more; those belong to full [second-order logic](c:second-order-logic).
examples: Connectivity of a graph is expressible: for every nonempty proper set $X$ of vertices, some edge joins $X$ to its complement.
Three-colorability of a graph is expressible: there are sets $X_1,X_2,X_3$ that cover the vertices, and no edge has both ends in one set.
Non-example: on a finite set with no relations, the property that the universe has an even number of elements is not expressible in monadic second-order logic.

steps: Take a [first-order](c:first-order-logic) formula $\varphi$ over a relational signature.
It quantifies over elements only, so it contains no set quantifier.
So $\varphi$ is also a monadic second-order formula, with the same meaning.
links.why: Every first-order property is a monadic second-order property.

steps: Take a monadic second-order formula.
A set variable is a relation variable of arity $1$, so each set quantifier is a second-order quantifier.
So the formula is a [second-order](c:second-order-logic) formula, and the monadic case limits relation variables to arity $1$.
links.why: Results for second-order logic apply to the monadic fragment, which is much easier to decide.

reminder: A monic polynomial is a nonzero polynomial whose leading coefficient is $1$.
definition: Let $R$ be a [ring](c:ring). A monic polynomial in $R[x]$ is a [polynomial](c:polynomial) $x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0$ with all $a_i\in R$, so the coefficient of its highest power of $x$ is $1$. A product of monic polynomials is monic, and a number that is a [root](c:root) of a monic polynomial over $\mathbb Z$ is an [algebraic integer](c:algebraic-integer).
examples: $x^2-2$ and $x^3+5x$ are monic in $\mathbb Z[x]$.
The minimal polynomial of an algebraic number over $\mathbb Q$ is monic by definition.
The characteristic polynomial $\det(xI-A)$ of a square matrix $A$ is monic.
Non-example: $2x^2+1$ is not monic in $\mathbb Z[x]$, because its leading coefficient is $2$.

reminder: Monodromy is the action of the loops of a base space on the fiber of a covering, by lifting each loop.
definition: Let $p\colon E\to X$ be a [covering space](c:covering-space) and $x\in X$. A loop $\gamma$ at $x$ lifts uniquely to a path in $E$ that starts at a given point $e$ of the fiber $p^{-1}(x)$, and its end point is again in the fiber. The rule $e\mapsto e\cdot[\gamma]$ is a [group action](c:group-action) of the [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) $\pi_1(X,x)$ on the fiber, a right action with this convention, called the monodromy.
examples: For the covering $\mathbb R\to S^1$, the fiber over $1$ is $\mathbb Z$, and the generator of $\pi_1(S^1)=\mathbb Z$ acts by $n\mapsto n+1$.
For the covering $z\mapsto z^2$ of $\mathbb C^\times$, the loop around $0$ swaps the two square roots of a point.
A trivial covering $X\times F\to X$ has trivial monodromy.
Non-example: $x\mapsto x^2$ on $\mathbb R$ is not a covering, because the fiber over $1$ has two points and the fiber over $0$ has one, so paths do not lift to give an action on a fiber.

steps: A [group action](c:group-action) of a group $G$ on a set $F$ gives a permutation of $F$ for each element of $G$.
Take $G=\pi_1(X,x)$ and $F=p^{-1}(x)$.
Lifting a loop and taking its end point permutes $F$, and the permutation depends only on the homotopy class of the loop.
These permutations compose as the loops compose, so lifting is an action of $\pi_1(X,x)$ on $F$.
links.why: Orbits of the monodromy action are the connected components of the covering space.

reminder: A monoidal category has a tensor product and a unit object that are associative and unital up to coherent isomorphisms.
definition: A monoidal category is a [category](c:category) $\mathcal C$ with a [functor](c:functor) $\otimes\colon\mathcal C\times\mathcal C\to\mathcal C$, a unit object $I$, and [natural isomorphisms](c:natural-isomorphism) $\alpha_{X,Y,Z}\colon(X\otimes Y)\otimes Z\to X\otimes(Y\otimes Z)$, $\lambda_X\colon I\otimes X\to X$ and $\rho_X\colon X\otimes I\to X$. They must satisfy the pentagon equation for four objects and the triangle equation for $X,I,Y$, which make every diagram built from them commute.
examples: Sets with the cartesian product and a one-point set as unit.
Vector spaces over a field $k$ with the tensor product $\otimes_k$ and unit $k$.
The endofunctors of a category, with composition as tensor product and the identity functor as unit.
Non-example: on sets, put $X\otimes Y=X\times Y\times Y$. For two-element sets, $(X\otimes Y)\otimes Z$ has $32$ elements and $X\otimes(Y\otimes Z)$ has $128$, so no associator exists.

steps: Take a [braided monoidal category](c:braided-monoidal-category) $\mathcal C$.
Forget the braiding $c_{X,Y}\colon X\otimes Y\to Y\otimes X$ and keep the tensor product, the unit and the associator.
What remains satisfies the pentagon and triangle equations, so $\mathcal C$ is a monoidal category.
links.why: A result for monoidal categories applies to every braided one.

steps: Take a [cartesian monoidal category](c:cartesian-monoidal-category), whose tensor product is the categorical product and whose unit is a terminal object.
The universal property of products gives canonical isomorphisms $(X\times Y)\times Z\cong X\times(Y\times Z)$ and $1\times X\cong X$.
These canonical isomorphisms satisfy the pentagon and triangle equations, because two maps into a product agree when they agree on each factor.
So it is a monoidal category, with the extra property that the tensor product is a product.
links.why: General monoidal tools apply to cartesian monoidal categories such as sets.

steps: Take a [monoid](c:monoid) $M$ and view it as a discrete category whose objects are the elements of $M$.
Define $x\otimes y=xy$ and let the unit object be the identity element of $M$.
Associativity and the unit laws of $M$ hold as equalities, so the associator and the unitors are identities.
The pentagon and triangle equations then hold trivially, so $M$ is a monoidal category.
links.why: A monoid is a monoidal category with only identity morphisms, and a monoidal category is a monoid up to isomorphism.

reminder: A monotone subsequence is a subsequence whose terms never decrease, or never increase.
definition: A monotone subsequence of a [sequence](c:sequence) $(a_i)$ in an ordered set is a [subsequence](c:subsequence) $(a_{i_1},a_{i_2},\dots)$, with $i_1<i_2<\cdots$, that is a [monotone sequence](c:monotone-sequence): either $a_{i_1}\le a_{i_2}\le\cdots$ or $a_{i_1}\ge a_{i_2}\ge\cdots$. The same definition applies to finite sequences, as in the Erdős-Szekeres theorem.
examples: In $(3,1,4,1,5,9,2,6)$, the terms $1,4,5,9$ in positions $2,3,5,6$ form an increasing subsequence.
Every sequence of real numbers has a monotone subsequence, which is the key step in a proof of the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem.
Non-example: in $(2,7,1,8)$, the subsequence $(2,7,1)$ is neither increasing nor decreasing.

steps: Take a monotone subsequence $(a_{i_1},a_{i_2},\dots)$ of $(a_i)$.
Its indices satisfy $i_1<i_2<\cdots$, so it is a [subsequence](c:subsequence) of $(a_i)$.
The monotone case adds that its terms never decrease, or never increase.
links.why: Facts about subsequences, such as a shared limit, apply to monotone subsequences.

reminder: A space is $n$-connected when it is path connected and its homotopy groups $\pi_k$ are trivial for $1\le k\le n$.
definition: Let $n\ge0$. A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is $n$-connected when it is nonempty and [path connected](c:path-connected-space), and the [homotopy group](c:homotopy-group) $\pi_k(X,x)$ is trivial for every $x\in X$ and every $1\le k\le n$. So $0$-connected means path connected, and $1$-connected means [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space).
examples: The sphere $S^m$ is $(m-1)$-connected for $m\ge1$.
Every [contractible space](c:contractible-space), such as $\mathbb R^m$, is $n$-connected for every $n$.
Non-example: $S^1$ is $0$-connected but not $1$-connected, because $\pi_1(S^1)=\mathbb Z$.

steps: Take a [simply connected space](c:simply-connected-space) $X$.
It is path connected, and its fundamental group $\pi_1(X,x)$ is trivial.
So $\pi_k(X,x)$ is trivial for $1\le k\le1$, and $X$ is $1$-connected.
links.why: Simply connected is the case $n=1$, so results for $n$-connected spaces start there.

steps: Take a [contractible space](c:contractible-space) $X$.
It is homotopy equivalent to a point, so it is path connected and $\pi_k(X,x)=0$ for all $k\ge1$.
Hence $X$ is $n$-connected for every $n$.
links.why: A contractible space satisfies every connectivity hypothesis, for all $n$ at once.

reminder: A group is nilpotent when its lower central series reaches the trivial subgroup after finitely many steps.
definition: The [lower central series](c:lower-central-series) of a [group](c:group) $G$ is $\gamma_1=G$ and $\gamma_{k+1}=[\gamma_k,G]$, the [subgroup](c:subgroup) generated by the commutators $[a,g]$ with $a\in\gamma_k$ and $g\in G$; so $\gamma_2$ is the [commutator subgroup](c:commutator-subgroup). The group $G$ is nilpotent when $\gamma_{c+1}=1$ for some $c\ge0$, and the least such $c$ is its class.
examples: Every [abelian group](c:abelian-group) is nilpotent, of class at most $1$.
The Heisenberg group of upper unitriangular $3\times3$ matrices is nilpotent of class $2$.
Every finite $p$-group is nilpotent.
Non-example: $S_3$ is not nilpotent, because $\gamma_2=A_3$ and $\gamma_3=[A_3,S_3]=A_3$, so the series never reaches $1$.

steps: Take an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $G$.
Every commutator $[a,g]$ is the identity, so $\gamma_2=[G,G]=1$.
So the lower central series reaches $1$ after one step, and $G$ is nilpotent of class at most $1$.
links.why: Nilpotent groups are the groups that are abelian layer by layer, so abelian arguments extend to them by induction.

steps: Take a nilpotent group $G$ with $\gamma_{c+1}=1$, and let $G^{(0)}=G$ and $G^{(k+1)}=[G^{(k)},G^{(k)}]$ be its derived series.
By induction $G^{(k)}\subseteq\gamma_{k+1}$, because $[G^{(k)},G^{(k)}]\subseteq[\gamma_{k+1},G]=\gamma_{k+2}$.
So $G^{(c)}\subseteq\gamma_{c+1}=1$, and $G$ is [solvable](c:solvable-group).
links.why: Every nilpotent group is solvable, so solvable group results apply to nilpotent groups.

reminder: The normal curvature in direction $v$ is the signed curvature of the plane section through $v$ and the surface normal.
definition: Let $S\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a regular surface with unit normal $N$ at a point $p$, and let $v\in T_pS$ be a unit tangent vector. The normal curvature $\kappa_n(v)$ is $\langle\gamma''(0),N\rangle$ for any unit-speed curve $\gamma$ in $S$ with $\gamma(0)=p$ and $\gamma'(0)=v$. It equals $\mathrm{II}(v,v)$, the value of the [second fundamental form](c:second-fundamental-form) on $v$, and it is the signed [curvature](c:curvature) at $p$ of the plane curve in which the plane spanned by $v$ and $N$ cuts $S$.
examples: On a sphere of radius $r$, the normal curvature has absolute value $1/r$ in every direction.
On a cylinder of radius $r$, the normal curvature is $0$ along the axis, and in a direction at angle $\theta$ from the axis it has absolute value $\sin^2\theta/r$.
By Meusnier's theorem, a curve on $S$ with curvature $\kappa$, whose principal normal makes angle $\theta$ with $N$, has normal curvature $\kappa\cos\theta$ in its tangent direction.
Non-example: the curvature $\kappa$ of a curve on $S$ is not the normal curvature of $S$; they agree only when the principal normal of the curve is $\pm N$.

reminder: An open manifold is a manifold without boundary in which no connected component is compact.
definition: An open manifold is a [manifold](c:manifold) without [boundary](c:boundary) all of whose [connected components](c:connected-component) are non-[compact](c:compact-space). No nonempty [closed manifold](c:closed-manifold) is an open manifold, because a closed manifold is compact.
examples: $\mathbb R^n$, and every open subset of $\mathbb R^n$, is an open manifold.
The cylinder $S^1\times\mathbb R$ is an open manifold.
Non-example: the $2$-sphere and the torus are compact, so they are not open manifolds.
Non-example: the disjoint union of $\mathbb R$ and a circle is not an open manifold, because its circle component is compact.

steps: Take an open manifold $M$.
By definition $M$ is a [manifold](c:manifold) without boundary.
The open case adds that every connected component of $M$ is non-compact.
links.why: Theorems for manifolds apply to open manifolds, and some, such as the h-principle, need openness.

reminder: An orthogonal matrix $A$ is a real square matrix with $A^TA=I$.
definition: An orthogonal matrix is a real [square matrix](c:square-matrix) $A$ whose [transpose](c:transpose-matrix) is its [inverse](c:inverse-matrix), that is $A^TA=AA^T=I$. Equivalently, the columns of $A$ form an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb R^n$, so $A$ preserves lengths and angles.
examples: The rotation matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&-\sin t\\\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}$.
Every [permutation matrix](c:permutation-matrix).
The reflection matrix $\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is not orthogonal, because $A^TA=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\ne I$.

steps: Take a [permutation matrix](c:permutation-matrix) $P$, which has exactly one entry $1$ in each row and column and zeros elsewhere.
Its columns are distinct standard basis vectors, so they are orthonormal.
Orthonormal columns give $P^TP=I$, so $P$ is orthogonal.
links.why: Every result for orthogonal matrices, such as preserving length, holds for permutation matrices.

reminder: An orthogonal transformation of a real inner product space is a linear map that preserves the inner product.
definition: Let $V$ be a real [inner product space](c:inner-product-space). An orthogonal transformation of $V$ is a [linear map](c:linear-map) $T\colon V\to V$ with $\langle Tx,Ty\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$ for all $x,y\in V$; equivalently, $T$ preserves norms, $\|Tx\|=\|x\|$. In an orthonormal basis of a finite-dimensional $V$, its matrix is an [orthogonal matrix](c:orthogonal-matrix).
examples: A rotation of $\mathbb R^2$ about the origin.
A reflection $x\mapsto x-2\langle x,u\rangle u$ in the hyperplane orthogonal to a unit vector $u$.
The identity map, and $-\mathrm{id}$.
Non-example: the projection $(x,y)\mapsto(x,0)$ is linear, but it sends the unit vector $(0,1)$ to $0$, so it is not orthogonal; scaling by $2$ doubles lengths.

steps: Take an orthogonal transformation $T$ and vectors $x,y$.
By linearity and norm preservation, $\|Tx-Ty\|=\|T(x-y)\|=\|x-y\|$.
So $T$ preserves distances, and it is an [isometry](c:isometry) of $V$.
The orthogonal case adds that $T$ is linear, so it fixes $0$.
links.why: An orthogonal transformation is an isometry that fixes the origin, and every isometry fixing $0$ is orthogonal.

steps: Take an [orthogonal matrix](c:orthogonal-matrix) $A$ and define $T(x)=Ax$ on $\mathbb R^n$ with the standard inner product.
Then $\langle Tx,Ty\rangle=x^TA^TAy$.
Since $A^TA=I$, this equals $x^Ty=\langle x,y\rangle$.
So $T$ is an orthogonal transformation.
links.why: Matrix results for orthogonal matrices carry over to the coordinate-free setting.

reminder: An outer measure gives every subset a value in $[0,\infty]$, is monotone and countably subadditive, and gives the empty set $0$.
definition: An outer measure on a [set](c:set) $X$ is a function $\mu^*$ on the [power set](c:power-set) of $X$ with values in $[0,\infty]$ such that $\mu^*(\emptyset)=0$, $\mu^*(A)\le\mu^*(B)$ whenever $A\subseteq B$, and $\mu^*\big(\bigcup_nA_n\big)\le\sum_n\mu^*(A_n)$ for every [countable](c:countable-set) family $(A_n)$ of subsets. It need not be additive; Carathéodory's construction picks the sets on which it is additive, and these form a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra).
examples: The Lebesgue outer measure on $\mathbb R$ is $\lambda^*(A)=\inf\sum_k(b_k-a_k)$ over countable covers of $A$ by intervals $(a_k,b_k)$.
The function that is $0$ on the empty set and $1$ on every other subset is an outer measure.
Non-example: $A\mapsto|A|^2$ on finite sets is not an outer measure, because $|\{1,2\}|^2=4$ is larger than $|\{1\}|^2+|\{2\}|^2=2$, so it is not subadditive.

reminder: A partitioned matrix is a matrix cut into rectangular blocks by partitioning its row indices and its column indices.
definition: Let $A\colon I\times J\to X$ be a [matrix](c:matrix) with row index set $I$ and column index set $J$. A partitioned, or block, matrix is $A$ together with a [partition](c:finpartition) $I=\bigsqcup_kI_k$ of the rows and a partition $J=\bigsqcup_lJ_l$ of the columns. The blocks are the submatrices $A_{kl}=A|_{I_k\times J_l}$, and one writes $A=(A_{kl})$.
examples: A $4\times4$ matrix cut after row $2$ and after column $2$ gives four $2\times2$ blocks $\begin{pmatrix}B&C\\D&E\end{pmatrix}$.
A block diagonal matrix is a partitioned matrix whose off-diagonal blocks are zero.
The [Schur complement](c:schur-complement) $D-CA^{-1}B$ is defined from the four blocks of a partitioned matrix $\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}$.
Non-example: cutting the rows of a $3\times3$ matrix into the groups $\{1,2\}$ and $\{2,3\}$ is not a partition, because row $2$ lies in both groups.

reminder: A periodic orbit is an orbit of a dynamical system that returns to its starting point after a fixed positive time.
definition: For a [dynamical system](c:dynamical-system) given by a map $f\colon X\to X$, the [orbit](c:orbit) of $x$ is periodic when $f^n(x)=x$ for some $n\ge1$, and the least such $n$ is its period. For a [flow](c:flow) $\varphi_t$, the orbit of a point $x$ that is not an equilibrium is periodic when $\varphi_T(x)=x$ for some $T>0$, and the least such $T$ is its period; the orbit is then a closed curve.
examples: For $\dot x=-y$, $\dot y=x$, every circle $x^2+y^2=r^2$ with $r>0$ is a periodic orbit of period $2\pi$.
For the logistic map $f(x)=3.2\,x(1-x)$, there is an attracting periodic orbit of period $2$.
A rotation of the circle by the angle $2\pi p/q$, in lowest terms, makes every orbit periodic of period $q$.
Non-example: an equilibrium of a flow is a fixed point, not a periodic orbit; a spiral that approaches a circle without closing up never returns to its start.

steps: Take a [fixed point](c:fixed-point) $x$ of a map $f$, so that $f(x)=x$.
Then $f^1(x)=x$, so the orbit $\{x\}$ is periodic with $n=1$.
So the fixed points are the periodic orbits of period $1$.
links.why: Fixed point results are the period-one case, and periodic orbits of period $n$ are fixed points of $f^n$.

reminder: The permanent of a square matrix is the sum over all permutations of the products of its entries, with no signs.
definition: For an $n\times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) $A=(a_{ij})$ over a [commutative semiring](c:comm-semiring), the permanent is $\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^na_{i,\sigma(i)}$, where $S_n$ is the [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group). It is the formula of the [determinant](c:determinant) without the signs $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$.
examples: $\operatorname{per}\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}=ad+bc$.
For the $n\times n$ matrix of all ones, the permanent is $n!$.
For the biadjacency matrix of a [bipartite graph](c:bipartite-graph) with $n+n$ vertices, the permanent counts the [perfect matchings](c:perfect-matching).
Non-example: the determinant is not the permanent; for the $2\times2$ matrix of all ones, $\det=0$ but $\operatorname{per}=2$.

steps: Take the [immanant](c:immanant) $\operatorname{Imm}_\chi(A)=\sum_\sigma\chi(\sigma)\prod_ia_{i,\sigma(i)}$ for a character $\chi$ of $S_n$.
Choose the trivial character, $\chi(\sigma)=1$ for all $\sigma$.
Then every term has coefficient $1$, and the sum is $\sum_\sigma\prod_ia_{i,\sigma(i)}$.
This sum is the permanent; the sign character gives the determinant instead.
links.why: The permanent and the determinant are the two extreme immanants, and results for immanants apply to both.

reminder: A permutation matrix is a square matrix with exactly one entry $1$ in each row and column and zeros elsewhere.
definition: A permutation matrix is a [square matrix](c:square-matrix) with entries in $\{0,1\}$ that has exactly one $1$ in each row and exactly one $1$ in each column. For a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, the matrix $P_\sigma$ with $(P_\sigma)_{ij}=1$ exactly when $i=\sigma(j)$ sends the basis vector $e_j$ to $e_{\sigma(j)}$.
examples: The identity matrix.
The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ swaps the two coordinates.
The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$ cycles the basis vectors.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has two entries $1$ in its first column, so it is not a permutation matrix.

steps: A [monomial matrix](c:monomial-matrix) has exactly one nonzero entry in each row and in each column.
A permutation matrix has exactly one entry $1$ in each row and column, and zeros elsewhere.
So it is a monomial matrix, whose nonzero entries all equal $1$.
links.why: Facts about monomial matrices apply to permutation matrices, which are monomial matrices without scaling.

steps: Take a permutation matrix $P$.
Its columns are distinct standard basis vectors, so they are orthonormal.
Orthonormal columns mean $P^TP=I$, so $P$ is an [orthogonal matrix](c:orthogonal-matrix).
Permutation matrices add that all entries lie in $\{0,1\}$.
links.why: Permutation matrices preserve lengths and angles, and they form a finite subgroup of the orthogonal group.

reminder: The Poisson kernel $P_r(\theta)=\frac{1-r^2}{1-2r\cos\theta+r^2}$ turns boundary values on the unit circle into a harmonic function inside the disc.
definition: For $0\le r<1$, the Poisson kernel of the [unit disc](c:unit-disc) is $P_r(\theta)=\frac{1-r^2}{1-2r\cos\theta+r^2}=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}r^{|n|}e^{in\theta}$. If $f$ is a continuous function on the unit circle, then $u(re^{i\theta})=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}P_r(\theta-t)f(e^{it})\,dt$ is the [harmonic function](c:harmonic-function) on the disc with boundary values $f$. This integral is the [convolution](c:convolution) of $f$ with $P_r$ on the circle.
examples: $P_0(\theta)=1$, so the value $u(0)$ is the mean value of $f$ on the circle.
For $f(e^{it})=\cos t$, the integral gives $u(re^{i\theta})=r\cos\theta$.
On the upper half-plane, the Poisson kernel is $P_y(x)=\frac{y}{\pi(x^2+y^2)}$.

Non-example: the Dirichlet kernel $D_n(\theta)=\sin((n+\tfrac12)\theta)/\sin(\theta/2)$ takes negative values and is not a Poisson kernel; its convolutions are partial Fourier sums, not harmonic extensions.

steps: Take the functions $\delta_r=\frac1{2\pi}P_r$ for $0\le r<1$.
Each $\delta_r$ is positive and has integral $1$ over the circle.
For each $\eta>0$, the integral of $\delta_r$ over $|\theta|>\eta$ tends to $0$ as $r\to1$.
So $(\delta_r)$ is an [approximation to the identity](c:approximation-of-the-identity) as $r\to1$.
links.why: Because of this, the harmonic extension of a continuous $f$ tends to $f$ at the boundary.

reminder: A polynomial identity is an equation between polynomials that holds after every substitution of values for the variables.
definition: A polynomial identity is an equation $P=Q$ between [polynomials](c:polynomial) that holds as an identity, meaning $P-Q$ is the zero polynomial, so both sides agree after every substitution of elements of a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring). In ring theory, a polynomial identity of an [algebra](c:algebra) $A$ is a nonzero noncommutative polynomial $f(x_1,\dots,x_n)$, an element of a [free algebra](c:free-algebra), with $f(a_1,\dots,a_n)=0$ for all $a_i\in A$.
examples: $(x+y)^2=x^2+2xy+y^2$ holds in every commutative ring.
Euler's four-square identity writes the product $(a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2+a_4^2)(b_1^2+b_2^2+b_3^2+b_4^2)$ as a sum of four squares of bilinear expressions in the $a_i$ and $b_i$.

The commutator $xy-yx$ is a polynomial identity of every commutative algebra, and the standard polynomial $s_4$ is a polynomial identity of the algebra of $2\times2$ matrices, by the Amitsur-Levitzki theorem.
Non-example: $x^2=1$ holds for $x=\pm1$ in $\mathbb R$ but not for every $x$, so it is an equation but not a polynomial identity.

reminder: A holomorphic line bundle is positive when it has a Hermitian metric whose curvature form, times $i$, is a positive $(1,1)$-form.
definition: Let $L$ be a holomorphic [line bundle](c:line-bundle) on a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) $X$. It is positive when $L$ has a Hermitian metric $h$ whose [curvature](c:curvature) form $\Theta_h$ makes $i\Theta_h$ a positive definite $(1,1)$-form. On a compact $X$, this means that the first [Chern class](c:chern-class) $c_1(L)$ is represented by a Kähler form.
examples: The hyperplane bundle $\mathcal O(1)$ on [complex projective space](c:complex-projective-space), with the Fubini-Study metric, is positive.
Positive powers $\mathcal O(k)$ with $k>0$, and tensor products of positive bundles, are positive.
A holomorphic line bundle of positive degree on a compact Riemann surface is positive.
Non-example: the tautological bundle $\mathcal O(-1)$ has negative curvature, and on a compact manifold the trivial bundle is not positive, because $c_1=0$ is not a Kähler class.

steps: Take a positive line bundle $L$ on a complex manifold $X$.
By definition $L$ is a holomorphic [line bundle](c:line-bundle) on $X$.
The positive case adds a Hermitian metric $h$ for which $i\Theta_h$ is a positive $(1,1)$-form.
links.why: Positivity is the extra hypothesis that gives vanishing and embedding theorems for line bundles.

reminder: A state of a Markov chain is positive recurrent when the chain returns to it with probability $1$ and the mean return time is finite.
definition: Let $(X_n)$ be a [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) on a countable state space, and let $T_i=\inf\{n\ge1:X_n=i\}$ be the return time to a state $i$, a [stopping time](c:stopping-time). The state $i$ is positive recurrent when $\mathbb P_i(T_i<\infty)=1$ and the [expected value](c:expected-value) $\mathbb E_i[T_i]$ is finite. An irreducible chain has a stationary distribution exactly when it is positive recurrent.
examples: Every state of an irreducible Markov chain with finitely many states is positive recurrent.
The walk on $\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that moves up with probability $p$, moves down with probability $1-p$, and stays at $0$ when it would go below $0$, is positive recurrent for $p<1/2$.
Non-example: the simple symmetric random walk on $\mathbb Z$ returns to $0$ with probability $1$, but $\mathbb E_0[T_0]=\infty$, so it is null recurrent and not positive recurrent.

reminder: Projective space $\mathbb P(V)$ is the set of lines through the origin in a vector space $V$.
definition: For a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over a [field](c:field) $k$, the projective space is $\mathbb P(V)=(V\setminus\{0\})/k^\times$, the [quotient space](c:quotient-space) in which $v\sim\lambda v$ for every nonzero scalar $\lambda$. Its points are the one-dimensional subspaces of $V$, and $\mathbb P^n(k)=\mathbb P(k^{n+1})$ has dimension $n$, with homogeneous coordinates $[x_0:\cdots:x_n]$.
examples: $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb R)$ is a circle, and $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)$ is the Riemann sphere.
$\mathbb P^2(\mathbb R)$ is the set of lines through the origin in $\mathbb R^3$.
Affine space $k^n$ sits inside $\mathbb P^n(k)$ as the points with $x_0\ne0$.
Non-example: the unit sphere $S^n\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is not $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb R)$, because $v$ and $-v$ stay distinct and $S^n\to\mathbb P^n(\mathbb R)$ is a two-to-one cover.

steps: Take $V=\mathbb C^{n+1}$ over the field $\mathbb C$.
Then $\mathbb P(V)$ is the space of complex lines through the origin of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$.
This space is [complex projective space](c:complex-projective-space) $\mathbb{CP}^n$.
links.why: General facts about projective space give the basic facts about complex projective space.

steps: Take $V=\mathbb R^{n+1}$ over the field $\mathbb R$.
Then $\mathbb P(V)$ is the space of real lines through the origin of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$.
This space is [real projective space](c:real-projective-space) $\mathbb{RP}^n$.
links.why: General facts about projective space give the basic facts about real projective space.

reminder: A provability predicate is an arithmetic formula $\mathrm{Prov}_T(x)$ that holds exactly when the sentence with code $x$ is a theorem of $T$.
definition: Let $T$ be a recursively axiomatized [first-order theory](c:first-order-theory) that extends [Peano arithmetic](c:peano-arithmetic), and fix a [Gödel numbering](c:godel-numbering) of its sentences and proofs. The provability predicate is the formula $\mathrm{Prov}_T(x)=\exists p\,\mathrm{Proof}_T(p,x)$, where the decidable arithmetical formula $\mathrm{Proof}_T(p,x)$ says that $p$ codes a $T$-proof of the sentence with code $x$. It is a $\Sigma_1$ formula that is true in the standard model exactly for the codes of theorems of $T$, and it satisfies the Hilbert-Bernays-Löb derivability conditions.
examples: The consistency statement of $T$ is the sentence $\neg\mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner0=1\urcorner)$, which Gödel's second incompleteness theorem is about.
Löb's theorem says that if $T\vdash\mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner\varphi\urcorner)\to\varphi$, then $T\vdash\varphi$.
Non-example: a truth predicate for arithmetic is not a provability predicate, because by Tarski's theorem no arithmetical formula defines the set of codes of true sentences.

reminder: A pseudodifferential operator multiplies the Fourier transform of $u$ by a symbol $a(x,\xi)$ and then transforms back.
definition: A pseudodifferential operator of order $m$ on $\mathbb R^n$ is an operator $Pu(x)=(2\pi)^{-n}\int e^{ix\cdot\xi}a(x,\xi)\,\hat u(\xi)\,d\xi$, where $\hat u$ is the [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) of $u$ and the symbol $a$ is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) with $|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^\beta a(x,\xi)|\le C_{\alpha\beta}(1+|\xi|)^{m-|\beta|}$. These operators include every [differential operator](c:differential-operator), whose symbol is a polynomial in $\xi$, and the principal symbol of a composition is the product of the principal symbols.
examples: A differential operator $\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}a_\alpha(x)D^\alpha$ has the symbol $\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}a_\alpha(x)\xi^\alpha$.
The operator $(1-\Delta)^{s/2}$ is a Fourier multiplier with symbol $(1+|\xi|^2)^{s/2}$, of order $s$.
An elliptic differential operator of order $m$ has an inverse modulo smoothing operators, and this inverse is pseudodifferential of order $-m$.
Non-example: the Fourier multiplier with symbol $e^{|\xi|^2}$ is not pseudodifferential, because its symbol grows faster than every power of $|\xi|$.

steps: Take a [differential operator](c:differential-operator) $P=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}a_\alpha(x)D^\alpha$ with smooth coefficients.
By Fourier inversion, $Pu(x)=(2\pi)^{-n}\int e^{ix\cdot\xi}p(x,\xi)\,\hat u(\xi)\,d\xi$ with $p(x,\xi)=\sum a_\alpha(x)\xi^\alpha$.
The polynomial $p$ satisfies the symbol estimates of order $m$.
So $P$ is a pseudodifferential operator of order $m$.
links.why: Pseudodifferential operators allow inverses of elliptic operators, which differential operators do not.

steps: A [Fourier integral operator](c:fourier-integral-operator) has the form $Au(x)=\iint e^{i\phi(x,y,\xi)}a(x,y,\xi)\,u(y)\,dy\,d\xi$ for a phase $\phi$.
Take the phase $\phi(x,y,\xi)=(x-y)\cdot\xi$ and an amplitude $a(x,\xi)$ that does not depend on $y$.
Then $\int e^{-iy\cdot\xi}u(y)\,dy=\hat u(\xi)$, so $Au(x)$ is the operator $Pu(x)$ of the definition, up to the factor $(2\pi)^{-n}$.
links.why: Pseudodifferential operators are the Fourier integral operators whose phase has no change of variables.

reminder: A punctured neighborhood of a point $x$ is a neighborhood of $x$ with the point $x$ removed.
definition: Let $X$ be a [topological space](c:topological-space) and $x\in X$. A punctured neighborhood of $x$ is a set $U\setminus\{x\}$, where $U$ is a [neighborhood](c:neighborhood-2) of $x$; equivalently, it is the relative [complement](c:complement) of $\{x\}$ in $U$. Limits of functions at $x$ are taken over punctured neighborhoods, so the value at $x$ plays no role.
examples: In $\mathbb R$, $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\setminus\{x\}=(x-\varepsilon,x)\cup(x,x+\varepsilon)$.
In $\mathbb R^2$, an open disc without its center is a punctured neighborhood of the center.
The limit $\lim_{y\to0}\sin(y)/y=1$ uses only values on punctured neighborhoods of $0$, so the undefined value at $0$ does not matter.
Non-example: the full neighborhood $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)$ contains $x$, so it is not a punctured neighborhood of $x$.

reminder: The pushforward $f_*\mu$ gives a set $B$ the measure $\mu(f^{-1}(B))$ of its preimage.
definition: Let $(X,\mu)$ be a [measure space](c:measure-space), let $Y$ be a [measurable space](c:measurable-space), and let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a [measurable function](c:measurable-function). The pushforward measure $f_*\mu$ is the [measure](c:measure) on $Y$ with $(f_*\mu)(B)=\mu(f^{-1}(B))$ for every measurable $B\subseteq Y$, where $f^{-1}(B)$ is the [preimage](c:preimage). It satisfies $\int g\,d(f_*\mu)=\int g\circ f\,d\mu$ for every measurable $g\ge0$ on $Y$.
examples: The law of a random variable $X$ on a probability space $(\Omega,P)$ is the pushforward $X_*P$.
The map $x\mapsto2x$ pushes Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$ forward to $\tfrac12$ times Lebesgue measure on $[0,2]$.
The map $f$ pushes the Dirac measure $\delta_x$ forward to $\delta_{f(x)}$.
Non-example: if $f$ is not measurable, then $f^{-1}(B)$ may fail to be measurable, so $\mu(f^{-1}(B))$ is undefined and there is no pushforward measure.

steps: Take a probability space $(\Omega,P)$ and a [random variable](c:random-variable) $X\colon\Omega\to\mathbb R$.
The variable $X$ is a measurable function and $P$ is a measure, so the pushforward $X_*P$ is defined.
Its value on $B$ is $P(X\in B)$, the probability that $X$ lands in $B$.
So the [law](c:has-law) of $X$ is the pushforward $X_*P$.
links.why: Facts about pushforward measures give the law of a function of a random variable.
